{{Short description|Equations of electromagnetism}}
{{Electromagnetism|cTopic=Electrodynamics}}

In [[electromagnetism]], '''Jefimenko's equations''' (named after [[Oleg D. Jefimenko]]) describe the [[electric field]] and [[magnetic field|magnetic fields]] generated by time-dependent distributions of [[electric charge]] and [[electric current|current]]. These equations account for the [[Retarded time|propagation delay of the fields]] due to the finite [[speed of light]], and provide the general solution to [[Maxwell’s equations]] for any arbitrary distribution of sources. Jefimenko's equations are the time-dependent generalizations of [[Coulomb's law]] and the [[Biot–Savart law]].

An alternative formulation for the electric field by [[Wolfgang Panofsky]] and [[Melba Phillips]] is known as the '''Panofsky–Phillips equation'''. This equation is related to one of Jefimenko's equations via the [[continuity equation]] for charge.

A version of Jefimenko's equations with a [[Point particle|point-like]] electric charge as the source is known as the '''Heaviside–Feynman formula''' or '''Jefimenko–Feynman formula'''.

==Formulation==

=== Electric and magnetic fields ===
Jefimenko's equations describe the [[electric field]] '''<math>\mathbf{E}</math>''' and [[magnetic field]] '''<math>\mathbf B</math>''' produced by an arbitrary, time-dependent distributions of [[charge density]] <math>\rho</math> and [[current density]] <math>\mathbf{J}</math>:<ref name=":1">[[Oleg D. Jefimenko]], ''Electricity and Magnetism: An Introduction to the Theory of Electric and Magnetic Fields'', Appleton-Century-Crofts (New-York - 1966). 2nd ed.: Electret Scientific (Star City - 1989), {{ISBN|978-0-917406-08-9}}.</ref><ref name=":0">{{cite book |last=Griffiths |first=David J. |title=Introduction To Electrodynamics |date=1999 |publisher=Prentice Hall |isbn=81-7758-293-3 |edition=3rd |pages=427-438}}</ref>

: <math>
\mathbf{E}
=
\frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\,
\iiint
\left(
\frac{[\rho]\,\mathbf{n}}{r^2}
+
\frac{[\dot{\rho}]\,\mathbf{n}}{c\,r}
-
\frac{\left[\dot{\mathbf{J}}\right]}{c^2 r}
\right)
\, dV'
</math>

: <math>
\mathbf{B}
=
\frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\,
\displaystyle\iiint
\left(
\frac{\left[\mathbf{J}\right]\times\mathbf{n}}{c^2 r^2}
+
\frac{\left[\dot{\mathbf{J}}\right]\times\mathbf{n}}{c^3 r}
\right)
\, dV'
</math>


Here, <math>\varepsilon_0</math> is the [[vacuum permittivity]], '''<math>r = |\mathbf r-\mathbf r'|</math>''' is the distance between the source point '''<math>\mathbf r'</math>''' and the observation point '''<math>\mathbf r</math>''', and '''<math>\mathbf{n}</math>''' is the unit vector pointing from the source toward the observer.

Because electromagnetic disturbances propagate at the [[speed of light]] <math>c</math>, the fields observed at a point '''<math>\mathbf r</math>''' at time '''<math>t</math>''' are determined by the state of the sources at an earlier [[retarded time]], <math display="inline">t_r = (t - r/c)</math>. The square brackets <math>[\ldots]</math> indicate that the enclosed quantities are evaluated at retarded time:<blockquote><math>[\rho]=\rho\!\left(t-\displaystyle\frac{r}{c}\right)</math>  , <math>[\dot{\rho}]=\dot{\rho}\!\left(t-\displaystyle\frac{r}{c}\right)
</math>, <math>[\mathbf{J}]=\mathbf{J}\!\left(t-\displaystyle\frac{r}{c}\right)</math>  and   <math>\left[\dot{\mathbf{J}}\right]=\dot{\mathbf{J}}\!\left(t-\displaystyle\frac{r}{c}\right)</math></blockquote>In the [[electrostatic]] situation, the first term of the electric field equation reduces to the [[Coulomb's law]]. Similarly, in the [[magnetostatic]] limit, the first term of the magnetic field equation reduces to the [[Biot–Savart law]]. Jefimenko's equations are the time-dependent generalizations of these two laws.<ref>[[David J. Griffiths]], Mark A. Heald, ''Time-dependent generalizations of the Biot–Savart and Coulomb laws'', American Journal of Physics '''59 (2)''' (1991), 111-117.</ref>

=== Derivation from retarded potentials ===
Jefimenko's equations can be derived from the [[Retarded potential|retarded potentials]] V and '''A''':<ref name=":0" />
:<math>
V
=
\frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\,
\displaystyle\iiint
\left(
\frac{[\rho]}{r}
\right)
\, dV'
</math>

:<math>
\mathbf{A}
=
\frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0 c^2}\,
\displaystyle\iiint
\left(
\frac{\left[\mathbf{J}\right]}{r}
\right)
\, dV'
</math>
These potentials are the solutions to [[Maths of EM field#Potential field approach|Maxwell's equations in the potential formulation]] (see the [[Helmholtz decomposition|Helmholtz theorem]]). To obtain the fields, these expressions are substituted into the definitions of the electromagnetic potentials : 
:<math>
\mathbf{E}
=
-\boldsymbol{\operatorname{grad}}\!\left(V\right)
-
\frac{\partial \mathbf{A}}{\partial t}
</math>

:<math>
\mathbf{B}
=
\boldsymbol{\operatorname{rot}}\!\left(\mathbf{A}\right)
</math>
By performing the differentiations with respect to the observer's coordinates '''<math>\mathbf r</math>''' and time '''<math>t</math>''', the potentials are eliminated in favor of the direct functional dependence on the sources '''<math>\rho</math>''' and '''<math>\mathbf J</math>'''. The fields have an implicit dependence on the position through <math display="inline">t_r</math>, which must be taken into account in the differentiation.<ref name=":0" />

For the [[electric field]], the detailed calculation gives:<ref name="TheRelationBetweenPP.andJ." />

:<math>
-\boldsymbol{\operatorname{grad}}\!\left(V\right)
=
\frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\,
\iiint
\left(
\frac{[\rho]\,\mathbf{n}}{r^2}
+
\frac{[\dot{\rho}]\,\mathbf{n}}{c\,r}
\right)
\, dV'
</math>
:<math>
-
\frac{\partial \mathbf{A}}{\partial t}
=
-
\frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0 c^2}\,
\iiint
\left(
\frac{\left[\dot{\mathbf{J}}\right]}{r}
\right)
\, dV'
</math>

== Panofsky–Phillips equation ==
The equation for the electric field can be written in an alternative form by using the [[continuity equation]] for electric charge:<ref name="TheRelationBetweenPP.andJ.">{{cite journal |last=McDonald |first=Kirk T. |date=1997 |title=The relation between expressions for time-dependent electromagnetic fields given by Jefimenko and by Panofsky and Phillips |url= |journal=American Journal of Physics |volume=65 |issue=11 |pages=1074–1076 |doi=10.1119/1.18723 |issn=0002-9505 |access-date=}} Updated version 2018 https://kirkmcd.princeton.edu/examples/jefimenko.pdf. </ref><ref name=":02">Introduction to Electrodynamics (3rd Edition), D. J. Griffiths, Pearson Education, Dorling Kindersley, 2007, {{ISBN|81-7758-293-3}}.</ref>

: <math>\mathbf{E}
=
\frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}
\iiint
\left(
\frac{[\rho]\mathbf{n}}{r^2}
+
\frac{
\left([\mathbf{J}]\cdot\mathbf{n}\right)\mathbf{n}
+
\left([\mathbf{J}]\times\mathbf{n}\right)\times\mathbf{n}
}{c\,r^2}
+
\frac{
\left([\dot{\mathbf{J}}]\times\mathbf{n}\right)\times\mathbf{n}
}{c^2 r}
\right)
\, dV'</math>

This equation was published in 1962 by [[Wolfgang Panofsky]] and [[Melba Phillips]] in the second edition of the textbook ''Classical Electricity and Magnetism''<ref name=":2" /> and is sometimes known as the Panofsky–Phillips equation.<ref name="b587" /> Panofsky and Phillips also published in this textbook the same expression as Jefimenko for the magnetic field (equation 14-34).<ref name=":2" />

The three terms in the equation represent different physical contributions to the electric field. The first term is related to the position of the source charges at the retarded time, and corresponds to [[Coulomb's law]] evaluated at the retarded time. The second term is related to the [[velocity]] of the source charges at the retarded time. It provides a correction to the retarded Coulomb field by compensating retardation effects when the currents are constant in time (<math>\dot{\mathbf{J}}=0</math>). This term vanishes in stationary regime when both <math>\nabla\cdot\mathbf{J}=0</math> and <math>\dot{\mathbf{J}}=0</math>.<ref name="TheRelationBetweenPP.andJ." /> The third term is produced by the [[acceleration]] of the source charges, and is referred to as the ''acceleration field'' or as the ''radiation field''.<ref name=":0" />

=== Distinction between near field and radiated field ===
The terms of the Panofsky–Phillips equations can be separated into two categories: The "near field" terms have a '''<math>1/r^2</math>''' dependence, and are significant only in the immediate vicinity of the sources. The "far field" terms have a '''<math>1/r</math>''' dependence. Due to their slower decrease with distance, they dominate as one moves away from the sources (see [[Near and far field|near field and far field]]).

:<math>
\definecolor{vert}{RGB}{0,153,0}
\mathbf{E}
=
\frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\,
\displaystyle\iiint
\left(
{\color{vert}
\frac{[\rho]\mathbf{n}}{r^2}
+
\frac{
\left(\left[\mathbf{J}\right]\cdot\mathbf{n}\right)\mathbf{n}
+
\left(\left[\mathbf{J}\right]\times\mathbf{n}\right)\times\mathbf{n}
}{c\,r^2}
}
\mathbin{\color{red}{+}}
{\color{red}
\frac{
\left(\left[\dot{\mathbf{J}}\right]\times\mathbf{n}\right)\times\mathbf{n}
}{c^2 r}
}
\right)
\, dV'
</math>

:<math>
\definecolor{vert}{RGB}{0,153,0}
\mathbf{B}
=
\frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\,
\displaystyle\iiint
\left(
{\color{vert}
\frac{\left[\mathbf{J}\right]\times\mathbf{n}}{c^2 r^2}
}
\mathbin{\color{red}{+}}
{\color{red}
\frac{\left[\dot{\mathbf{J}}\right]\times\mathbf{n}}{c^3 r}
}
\right)
\, dV'
</math>

* <span style="color:green;">In green are the '''near fields''' (decaying as 1/r²)</span>.
* <span style="color:red;">In red are the '''radiated fields''' (decaying as 1/r)</span>.


In the far-field region, near fields can be neglected and the expressions of the emitted fields reduce to:<ref name=":2"></ref><ref name="b587">{{cite journal |last1=de Melo e Souza |first1=R. |last2=Cougo-Pinto |first2=M. V. |last3=Farina |first3=C. |last4=Moriconi |first4=M. |date=2009-01-01 |title=Multipole radiation fields from the Jefimenko equation for the magnetic field and the Panofsky-Phillips equation for the electric field |url=https://pubs.aip.org/ajp/article/77/1/67/1057982/Multipole-radiation-fields-from-the-Jefimenko |journal=American Journal of Physics |volume=77 |issue=1 |pages=67–72 |arxiv=0812.4679 |doi=10.1119/1.2990666 |issn=0002-9505 |access-date=2026-05-03}}</ref>

<!-- [[File:Onde électromagnétique dans l'espace.svg|thumb|right|upright=1.4|Propagation of radiated fields in space]] -->
[[File:Onde electromagnetique.svg|thumb|right|upright=1.4|Propagation of radiated fields in space]]

: <math>\mathbf{E}=\frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0 c^2}\,\displaystyle\iiint\left(\frac{\left(\left[\dot{\mathbf{J}}\right]\times\mathbf{n}\right)\times\mathbf{n}}{r}\right)\, dV'</math>
: <math>\mathbf{B}=\frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0 c^3}\,\displaystyle\iiint\left(\frac{\left[\dot{\mathbf{J}}\right]\times\mathbf{n}}{r}\right)\, dV'</math>


One therefore has <math>
\mathbf{E}\perp\mathbf{B}\perp\mathbf{n}
</math> , with '''E''' and '''B''' related by:

<div class="center">
<math>
\mathbf{B}
=
\frac{\mathbf{n}\times\mathbf{E}}{c}
</math>
</div>

The Panofsky–Phillips equation allows one to directly distinguish between near fields and radiated fields for the electric field—something that is not apparent in Jefimenko’s formulation. In Jefimenko's electric field equation, both the second and third terms appear to contribute to the far field because they scale with '''<math>1/r</math>'''. However, this is illusory; the longitudinal component of the third term cancels the '''<math>1/r</math>''' dependence of the second term, leaving only the transverse components to propagate as radiation.<ref name="TheRelationBetweenPP.andJ." /> Despite this complication, Jefimenko’s electric field equation is more compact and sometimes easier to use for calculations. One of the exceptions is the case of electric dipole radiation.<ref name="b587" />

==Heaviside–Feynman formula==
[[Image:Explanation of variables in Heaviside-Feynman formula.svg|thumb|350px|right|Explanation of the variables relevant for the Heaviside–Feynman formula.]]

The '''Heaviside–Feynman formula''', also known as the Jefimenko–Feynman formula, can be seen as the [[point particle|point-like]] electric charge version of Jefimenko's equations. It can be non-trivially deduced from them using [[Dirac function]]s, or using the [[Liénard-Wiechert potentials]].<ref name=":3">[https://feynmanlectures.caltech.edu/II_21.html#Ch21-S5 The Feynman Lectures on Physics - 21.5 The potentials of a moving charge; the general solution of Liénard and Wiechert]</ref> The formula provides a natural generalization of the [[Coulomb's law]] for cases where the source charge is moving:
<math display="block"> \mathbf{E} =  \frac{-q}{4\pi \varepsilon_0} \left[ \frac{\mathbf{e}_{r'}}{r'^2} + \frac{r'}{c} \frac{d}{dt} \left(\frac{\mathbf{e}_{r'}}{r'^2}\right)  +\frac{1}{c^2} \frac{d^2}{dt^2} \mathbf{e}_{r'}  \right] </math>
<math display="block"> \mathbf{B} = - \mathbf{e}_{r'} \times \frac{\mathbf{E}}{c} </math>
Here, <math> q</math> is the electric charge, <math>\mathbf{e}_{r'}</math> is a [[unit vector]] pointing from the observer to the charge and <math>r'</math> is the distance between observer and charge. Both of these quantities are evaluated at the retarded time <math> t - r'/c </math>.

[[Image:Diagram explaining charge position in the retarded time.svg|thumb|400px|right|Illustration of the retarded charge position for a particle moving in one spatial dimension: the observer sees the particle where it was, not where it is.]]
The first term in the formula for <math>\mathbf{E}</math> represents the Coulomb's law for the static electric field. The second term is the time derivative of the first Coulombic term multiplied by <math>r'/c</math> which is the propagation time of the electric field. Heuristically, this can be regarded as nature "attempting" to forecast what the present field would be by linear extrapolation to the present time.<ref name="FeynmanLectures">[https://feynmanlectures.caltech.edu/I_28.html#Ch28-S1-p10 The Feynman Lectures on Physics Vol. I Ch. 28: Electromagnetic Radiation]</ref> The last term, proportional to the second derivative of the vector <math>e_{r'}</math>, is sensitive to charge motion perpendicular to the line of sight. It can be shown that the electric field generated by this term is proportional to <math> a_{t}/r' </math>, where <math>a_t</math> is the transverse acceleration in the retarded time. As it decreases only as <math>1/r'</math> with distance compared to the standard <math>1/r'^2</math> Coulombic behavior, this term is responsible for the long-range electromagnetic radiation caused by the accelerating charge.

The Heaviside–Feynman formula allows, for example, the derivation of the [[Larmor formula]] for overall radiation power of the accelerating charge.<ref name=":4" />

== Interpretations ==
Maxwell's equations are often interpreted as suggesting that spatially varying electric and magnetic fields induce one another, resulting in propagating [[Electromagnetic radiation|electromagnetic waves]].<ref>{{cite journal |author=Kinsler, P. |year=2011 |title=How to be causal: time, spacetime, and spectra |journal=Eur. J. Phys. |volume=32 |issue=6 |page=1687 |arxiv=1106.1792 |bibcode=2011EJPh...32.1687K |doi=10.1088/0143-0807/32/6/022 |s2cid=56034806}}</ref> However, [[Oleg D. Jefimenko]] has argued that Maxwell's equations do not demonstrate a direct causal relationship between the fields as they are evaluated at the same instant in time.<ref name="e911">{{cite book |last=Jefimenko |first=Oleg D. |title=Causality, Electromagnetic Induction, and Gravitation |date=2000 |publisher=Electret Scientific Company |isbn=0-917406-23-0 |location=Star City |pages=3-16}}</ref>

Unlike in Maxwell equations, where both sides of the equality occur simultaneously, the fields on the left side of Jefimenko's equations are explicitly "caused" by the state of the sources at an earlier time. Under this interpretation, the electric and magnetic fields are not causing each other; instead, they are both effects of the same underlying cause: time-dependent electric charge and current distributions.<ref name="e911" />

== History ==
According to [[Andrew Zangwill]], the equations analogous to Jefimenko's but in the [[frequency domain]] were first derived by [[George Adolphus Schott]] in 1912.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Schott |first=G. A. |url=http://archive.org/details/electromagneticr00schouoft |title=Electromagnetic radiation |date=1912 |publisher=University Press |others= |location=Cambridge}}</ref><ref name=":4">Andrew Zangwill, Modern Electrodynamics, Cambridge University Press, 1st edition (2013), pp. 726–727, 765, 879–886, 910–911</ref> As pointed out by Kirk T. McDonald,<ref>Kirk T. McDonald, ''The relation between expressions for time-dependent electromagnetic fields given by Jefimenko and by Panofsky and Phillips'', American Journal of Physics '''65 (11)''' (1997), 1074-1076.</ref> The time-domain versions of the equations in the Panofsky–Phillips form appear first in 1962 in the second edition of [[Wolfgang K. H. Panofsky|Panofsky]] and [[Melba Phillips|Phillips]]'s classic textbook.<ref name=":2">Wolfgang K. H. Panofsky, Melba Phillips, ''Classical Electricity And Magnetism'', Addison-Wesley (2nd. ed - 1962), Section 14.3. The electric field is written in a slightly different - but completely equivalent - form. Reprint: Dover Publications (2005), {{ISBN|978-0-486-43924-2}}.</ref> According to [[David J. Griffiths]], Jefimenko's equations seem to have been first published by Oleg D. Jefimenko in 1966.<ref name=":0" /><ref name=":1" />

Heaviside–Feynman formula was published by Oliver Heaviside in 1904<ref name="i522">{{cite journal |last=Heaviside |first=Oliver |date=1904 |title=The Radiation from an Electron Moving in an Elliptic, or any Other Orbit |url=https://www.nature.com/articles/069342b0 |journal=Nature |volume=69 |issue=1789 |pages=342–343 |doi=10.1038/069342b0 |issn=0028-0836 |access-date=2026-05-05}}</ref> and was rediscovered by Richard Feynman in 1963.<ref name=":3" /><ref name=":4" />
